job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Grace Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm back in my parents' house in Carmarthen, in west Wales, with my dad, who teaches at the primary school, and my mum, who is a pharmacist. I start at nine with applications, then go for a long walk by the river, which helps me think. In the afternoons I update my CV and practise the design software I'll need. It's been six months since my civil engineering degree at Cardiff.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What was your final project, and your internships?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My final project was a flood defence design for a river town, and it got a first. I did one placement at a drainage consultancy and one with a county council's highways team, where I spent a month measuring potholes. I enjoyed the mix of calculations and walking on real sites. I've applied to around fifty firms, and had two interviews that didn't lead anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's fine with me. I've seen that tools save time on calculations, but someone still needs to walk the site and decide what's sensible. I'd tell friends not to worry, but not to relax too much either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm mostly calm. Civil engineering is slow and cautious by nature, and nothing in this world would make a bridge safer to design without a person signing it. My real worry is the waiting, which has gone on six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, mostly to consultancies and councils within an hour of home. I'd ask for feedback after my two interviews, because I want to know what went wrong. I'd also take a short course in a software package that firms use, since several job ads asked for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little impatience. I know I'm lucky: my parents support me and I have savings, so I'm not scared. I just want to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of your work did the consultancy already do with software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What did you learn from the interviews that didn't work out?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do while waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One firm said I was strong on the technical side but quiet in the group exercise. I'd say that's fair. I tend to listen first, which isn't a flaw on site, but it doesn't show in a thirty-minute exercise. So I'd practise speaking up earlier, without pretending to be someone else.

say: I'd tell friends tools save **time** on calculations, but someone still has to walk the site.
I'd say don't worry, but don't **relax** too much.
think: Civil engineering is slow and cautious, and a person still **signs** the design.
My real worry is the **waiting**, not the machines.
do: Apply to consultancies and **councils** within an hour of home.
Ask for **feedback** after my two interviews.
Take a short course in a **software package** firms ask for.
feel: **Calm** with some impatience, grateful for family and savings.
S0.quote: I tend to listen first, which isn't a flaw on site, but it doesn't show in a thirty-minute exercise.
fieldNote: She sees the **slow** nature of civil work as protection.
Calm rests on savings and family, not on denial, which suits her steady outlook.

steps.text: Send applications to consultancies and councils near Carmarthen weekly
Take a short course in a drainage design package
Ask my placement supervisor for interview practice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the kind of change we need to handle sensibly. Firms should train people to use the tools, and the profession should keep clear rules about who is responsible. I'd tell friends to learn the tools now and not wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel a little uneasy. Report drafting, checking calculations and writing up site notes are things graduates do, and software could do them. If firms hire fewer graduates, my job hunt gets harder. But somebody has to check the work, and I believe that can be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools more, especially for drafting reports, and make sure I check every figure myself. I'd aim for roles with site visits, like site engineer or inspection work. I'd also apply to the flood-risk team at the council, since climate adaptation is growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not anxious. It's the feeling you get before a new project: you don't know the details, but you can see the shape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your own placement tasks could software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use it now and then, for drafting emails and explaining code in spreadsheets. I'd never trust it on a design number without checking. At the consultancy, someone caught a unit error in an AI-written note, and everyone laughed. It stuck with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you describe your use of AI so far?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calculation checking, report writing, drawing updates. Those are exactly the starter tasks. What software won't do soon is stand in a muddy field with a landowner and explain why the embankment has to move.

say: I'd say we need to handle this **sensibly**, with clear rules about who is responsible.
I'd tell friends to learn the tools **now**.
think: Report drafting and checking are **graduate tasks**, so hiring could slow.
Somebody has to **check** the work, and that can be me.
do: Use AI tools for drafting reports and **check every figure** myself.
Aim for **site engineer** and inspection roles.
feel: **Uneasy**, but like the feeling before a new project: I can see the shape.
S1.quote: What software won't do soon is stand in a muddy field with a landowner and explain why the embankment has to move.
fieldNote: She picks **site-facing** roles as her edge.
The anecdote about a **unit error** explains her checking habit.
Climate adaptation work gives her a growth area.

steps.text: Use an AI assistant to draft reports and verify each number
Apply for site engineer and flood-risk roles at councils
Keep sending ten applications a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not ready, and I'd want governments, firms and universities to start working together now. I'd stay measured in public. Panic doesn't help anyone, but a clear plan would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be worried. Design, calculation and reporting are thinking work, and in two years software might do all of it. Site work lasts longer, until the robots arrive around 2031, but even that's not guaranteed. I'd have no time to build experience before the junior jobs thin out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any site-based job quickly, even a lower-paid one, because it keeps me on the hands-on side. I'd learn to use the AI tools properly and offer to help the team with them. I'd save every spare pound, and I'd stay with my parents rather than rent. I'd also look at a trades route, like a site surveyor or a planner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A tight chest, like before an exam. I'd also feel a bit guilty, because I'm better off than many, with a family home and savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years for AGI, robots after. What do you do first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I trust councils and universities more than big firms, honestly. They've no reason to sell me anything. But I wouldn't trust anyone to move fast enough, so I'd also make my own plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you trust to prepare for this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing is to talk with my parents, at the kitchen table. They'd have views, and my dad has seen how education adapts. Then I'd call my placement supervisor and say, I'll take anything on site, how can I get started.

say: I'd say we're not ready and **governments**, firms and universities should work together now.
think: Design and calculation are thinking work, and in two years software might do **all of it**.
I'd have no time to build **experience** before junior jobs thin out.
do: Take any **site-based** job quickly, even lower paid.
Learn AI tools properly and offer to help the **team**.
Save every spare pound and stay with my **parents**.
feel: **Anxious**, with a tight chest, and a bit guilty for being better off.
S2.quote: Panic doesn't help anyone, but a clear plan would.
fieldNote: She stays **measured**, but private worry is real.
She trusts councils and **universities** over big firms.
Guilt about her privileges shapes how she talks, and she still plans for herself.

steps.text: Take the first site-based job in south Wales, even at lower pay
Learn the AI tools well enough to teach the site team
Save every spare pound by staying at my parents' house
Ask my placement supervisor for site work leads

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough for professions to adapt. Institutions of civil engineers should rewrite what a graduate does, and firms should train people differently. I'd be hopeful in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel uneasy. It's a real change, but I could get a first job, build three or four years of experience and become a chartered engineer before AGI. That counts for a lot, since chartered engineers sign the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a first job at a consultancy, aim for chartership within four years and learn the AI tools in depth. I'd save part of my pay, and I'd look at a postgraduate course in flood risk, part-time. I'd also keep up my walking and my friends, because I'd need the balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better than the two-year one. It's like seeing a slow storm over the hills, where you check the forecast and carry a coat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would five years change about your first job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would let me do things in the right order: job, chartership, then a specialism. With two years I'd have to grab anything. Five years lets me be a bit more thoughtful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you use the extra time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. I'd use them every day by then, but with my own checks. I think the safest engineers will be those who understand both the maths and the machine, and I can be one.

say: I'd say five years is long enough for the **profession** to adapt and rewrite what a graduate does.
think: I'd feel **uneasy**, but a first job and chartership could happen before AGI.
Chartered engineers **sign** the work, which counts for a lot.
do: Take a first job at a **consultancy** and aim for chartership in four years.
Study part-time flood risk at **postgraduate** level.
Save part of my pay and keep up my **walking** and friends.
feel: Like seeing a slow storm over the hills: **carry a coat**.
S3.quote: The safest engineers will be those who understand both the maths and the machine, and I can be one.
fieldNote: Time lets her do things in the **right order**: job, chartership, specialism.
She thinks accountability, not skill, is her **moat**.
Balance and friends matter to her.

steps.text: Accept a graduate engineer role at a consultancy in Cardiff or Swansea
Start the chartered engineer route with a professional body
Use AI tools daily and keep a personal checking routine
Save a quarter of each pay cheque

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good length, as long as people use it. I'd tell friends to look after their careers, and to look after each other. In public, I'd be steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm quite calm. By 33 I could be a chartered engineer with a team, perhaps leading flood-defence projects. The tools will change many times, but the river stays the river.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build my career, buy a small house in Carmarthen with my partner, if I have one by then. I'd learn each new tool as it appears, and I'd keep my savings in simple, safe places. I'd also volunteer with a local flood group, because that's the kind of work that will still need people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite fine. It's like looking at the horizon on a clear day. A little distant, but not frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. What would your life look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My main worry would be the people in my area whose work isn't as protected. I'd think of the shop assistants and drivers in my town. With ten years there's time, but it needs politics to use it well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also worry about whether society is fair about it. If firms keep every gain, even a good career for me wouldn't feel right. That isn't about me, but it's on my mind.

say: I'd say ten years is a good length as long as people **use it**.
I'd tell friends to look after their careers and **each other**.
think: I'm quite **calm**: by 33 I could be a chartered engineer leading flood projects.
The tools will change, but the **river** stays the river.
do: Build my **career** and buy a small house in Carmarthen.
Learn each new **tool** as it appears and keep savings safe.
feel: Quite **fine**, like looking at a clear horizon.
S4.quote: The tools will change many times, but the river stays the river.
fieldNote: Ten years makes her **calm**, grounded in physical work.
Her worry shifts to **neighbours** whose work is less protected.
Fairness of gains matters to her centrist **pragmatism**.

steps.text: Work toward chartered status and lead a flood-defence team
Save a deposit for a small house in Carmarthen
Learn each new design tool as firms adopt it
Volunteer weekends with the local flood action group

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. I would have no time to learn the job before the junior work thinned out. What would help is clear plans from government, training that firms actually offer, and a first job where someone teaches me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: People assume top graduates have it easy. The waiting wears on you in ways you don't see. I'm doing fine, though. A short reply from a firm, even a no, would make a big difference.

headlineQuote: People assume top graduates have it easy. The waiting wears on you in ways you don't see.
portrait: Grace is **23**, a civil engineering graduate from Carmarthen, back at home with her teacher father and pharmacist mother.
She uses AI **now and then**, checks every number herself and trusts accountable, site-based work.
Her mood climbs with the warning time: steady at **calm** in slow worlds, anxious in the fast one.
She is pragmatic, trusts councils and universities more than big firms, and wants **fairness**.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI picture, because there would be no time to learn the job.
whatWouldHelp: Clear **government plans**, real training from firms and a first job with a teacher.
